data.title: 10-Year Treasury Yield Touches 5%, Pushed by Oil Surge — WSJ
data.description:
Chelsey Dulaney and Sam Goldfarb

The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield briefly broke above 5% as widening instability in the Middle East pushed up oil prices, deepening investor concerns about inflation.

The yield on the benchmark bond hit 5.012% in morning trading, according to Tradeweb, its highest intraday level since 2007. It then fell back to about 4.96% as bond buyers were drawn in by higher yields and oil prices ticked a bit lower off their highs.

The 10-year yield, which helps set borrowing costs for consumers and businesses, has only topped 5% on one other occasion since 2007. Investors have been selling government bonds for weeks as oil prices climb. Brent crude approached $110 a barrel after drone attacks led Saudi Arabia to shut down a key oil pipeline, a move likely to squeeze global oil supply.

With inflation on the rise, the Federal Reserve is on Wednesday expected to raise interest rates for the first time this year.

In stocks, some tech names and industrial shares sold off after leaders of three of the biggest AI companies called for development of the technology to be slowed down.

The Nasdaq pared early losses, down about 0.1% in midday trading amid concerns that demand for AI services and inputs like memory chips could come under pressure. Chip stocks fell around 5%. The Dow was down 0.2%.

This item is part of a Wall Street Journal live coverage event. The full stream can be found by searching P/WSJL (WSJ Live Coverage).

data.title: Novo Nordisk Is Dropping Some Weight. It Still Faces a Bigger Challenge. — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Mackenzie Tatananni

Novo Nordisk is slimming down-and by shortening its brand name, the Danish drugmaker is signaling a new chapter as it aims to be more than a heavyweight in the market for GLP-1 medications.

The company announced Monday that it will now go by Novo, although its legal name remains Novo Nordisk. Rebranding to the shorthand long used by analysts and investors gives the Danish drugmaker a distinct, consistent identity to connect with stakeholders, the company said.

Alongside these changes, the drugmaker refreshed the central tenets of the "Novo Way" to focus more sharply on competitiveness, innovation, and integrity. Of course, these goals remain mere promises until Novo translates them into its daily operations.

The company is hardly floundering, as it remains one of two clear powerhouses in the weight-loss market, sharing an effective duopoly with Eli Lilly. However, it has struggled to diversify beyond its core offering of weight-loss drugs, and concerns persist around its ability to return to growth next year.

Novo's Wegovy and Ozempic, approved for chronic weight management and diabetes, respectively, continue to drive the bulk of its revenue. Meanwhile, attempts to find the next blockbuster have fallen short. Shares sank in July after Novo's anti-inflammatory drug candidate failed to reduce the risk of heart attacks and other major cardiovascular events in a late-stage trial.

Deutsche Bank analyst Emmanuel Papadakis cut his rating on the shares to Sell from Hold at the end of August, saying the drug was "effectively out of the picture" following the trial miss while flagging concerns over a major patent cliff in the coming years.

Even before then, pressure was mounting. In 2025, the company executed the largest corporate layoff in Denmark's history, paired with the termination of its chief executive and a major board shake-up.

Longtime company veteran and new CEO Mike Doustdar is trying to improve Novo's trajectory. Since assuming the company's top role last year, Doustdar has undertaken a cost-savings plan that included sweeping job cuts.

Under his direction, Novo captured a first-mover advantage in oral GLP-1s by launching a pill form of Wegovy, mirroring its earlier success as the first to bring an injectable to market. Despite the explosive popularity of oral Wegovy, many analysts believe Lilly has taken the lead in the weight-loss drug market.

While both stocks trail the benchmark S&P 500 in 2026, Novo's U.S.-listed shares have dropped over 14% while Lilly's have gained 6.3%, underscoring just how difficult it has become for Novo to tip the scales back in its favor.

Write to Mackenzie Tatananni at mackenzie.tatananni@barrons.com

data.title: OBITUARY-Bob Mackie, fashion designer for the stars, dies at 87
data.description:
Hollywood designer Bob Mackie, known for making stars such as Cher and Elton John sparkle, died on Monday at 87, according to a post on his official Instagram account.

His career spanned five decades and included designing a Barbie doll clothes collection.

Born in 1939 into a middle-class family in Monterey Park, California, he was nominated for more than 30 Emmys, winning nine. He received Academy Award nominations for costumes worn in the films "Lady Sings the Blues," "Funny Lady," and "Pennies From Heaven."

"His genius and extraordinary designs will live on forever, continuing to bring beauty into this world," his team said in an Instagram post. His cause of death was not stated.

Mackie was known for sequins, rhinestones and glitter, but also humor. The highlight of his 11-year run for The Carol Burnett Show was the "curtain dress" worn by Burnett in a sketch parodying 1939 film classic "Gone with the Wind." The costume, now in the collection of the Smithsonian's American History Museum, included a brass curtain rod balanced on Burnett's shoulders and a bit of valance worn as a hat.

data.title: US natgas futures climb 2% on lower output, higher LNG exports
data.description:
Key points:
  • Cove Point maintenance from around Sept. 19 could curb exports by 0.8 bcfd
  • Lower 48 output hit a monthly record in August before slipping to a two-week low
  • Warmer-than-normal weather through Sept. 29 should keep air-conditioning gas burn elevated
  • Europe's TTF and Asia's JKM hover near 44-month highs amid global supply disruptions

By Scott DiSavino

U.S. natural gas futures climbed 2% on Monday on a drop in daily output and an increase in daily liquefied natural gas exports.

Front-month gas futures for October delivery on the New York Mercantile Exchange rose 5.8 cents, or 2.0%, to $2.889 per million British thermal units.

Financial firm LSEG said average gas output in the U.S. Lower 48 states rose to 113.4 billion cubic feet per day (bcfd) so far in September, up from a monthly record high of 112.2 bcfd in August.

On a daily basis, however, output was on track to decline to a two-week low of 112.8 bcfd on Monday.

Record output and mild spring weather have allowed energy firms to keep the amount of gas in inventory above the five-year (2021-2025) average since March.

But with hotter-than-normal weather last week, analysts said the amount of gas in storage likely slid to 3.6% above normal during the week ended September 11, down from 4.8% above normal in the previous week, according to estimates ahead of Thursday's weekly federal inventory report.

Meteorologists forecast the weather would remain mostly warmer through September 29, with power generators burning more gas than usual to keep air conditioners running. About 40% of U.S. power generation comes from gas-fired plants.

LSEG projected average gas demand in the Lower 48 states, including exports, would slide from 109.5 bcfd this week to 107.3 bcfd next week. Those forecasts were lower than LSEG's outlook on Friday.

LNG EXPORTS

Average gas flows to the nine big U.S. LNG export plants rose to 18.3 bcfd so far in September, up from 17.2 bcfd in August, but remained short of the monthly record high of 18.8 bcfd in April.

On a daily basis, LNG feedgas was on track to rise to a 20-week high of 18.7 bcfd on Friday.

U.S. energy firm Berkshire Hathaway Energy, however, has told customers that it plans to shut its 0.8-bcfd Cove Point LNG export plant in Maryland for a couple of weeks of annual maintenance starting around September 19.

The U.S. became the world's biggest LNG exporter in 2023, surpassing Australia and Qatar, as surging global prices fed demand for more low-cost U.S. gas.

Around the world, gas traded at 44-month highs of around $28 per mmBtu at the Dutch Title Transfer Facility benchmark in Europe and $25 at the Japan-Korea Marker (JKMc1) benchmark in Asia.

Global gas prices have spiked in recent years primarily due to supply disruptions linked to Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran this year.

Prices in the U.S. have not reacted much to the war in Iran because the U.S. produces all the gas it consumes domestically and U.S. LNG companies are already liquefying as much fuel as they can.

No matter how high global gas prices go, the U.S. cannot export much more LNG until units under construction enter service in coming months and years.

data.title: Mara Stock Tumbles, Strategy Pauses, and Bitcoin Faces a Key Test — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Mackenzie Tatananni

While headlines on artificial intelligence led the stock market on Monday, Bitcoin-linked stocks made news of their own.

Shares of Mara Holdings tumbled after J.P. Morgan double-downgraded the crypto miner and aspiring data center operator to Underweight from Overweight.

Analyst Richard Choe questioned the company's execution of its pivot, citing "diluted value creation" driven by a capital-light joint venture with private equity firm Starwood Capital Group.

Mara and Starwood partnered in February to convert select Bitcoin mining sites into high-performance enterprise and AI data centers. However, Choe noted that some of Mara's existing locations have smaller power capacities, making them less attractive for data center conversion.

Only compounding the challenge, acquiring low-cost land is becoming harder due to rising competition "and is unlikely to serve as a durable competitive advantage," Choe said.

Mara fell 2.6% to $11.67 on Monday. Heading into the session, Mara had gained 33% this year, handily outpacing the broader market. Choe has assigned the stock a $11 price target, down from $13 previously.

Software provider-turned Bitcoin whale Strategy had news of its own on Monday. The company disclosed that it hadn't purchased any Bitcoin in the preceding week, extending a dry spell from the end of August.

As of Sept. 13, Strategy held 845,050 Bitcoin purchased for an average price of $75,412 each. That means the company acquired them for a narrow premium to the current price of the crypto, which has risen 1.1% over the past 24 hours to $78,127, according to CoinDesk.

Rather than buy or sell Bitcoin, the company repurchased 1,420,467 shares of its common stock for $139.3 million in cash. The company maintains a separate U.S. dollar reserve to service dividends on its preferred stock and pay back debt. The company currently has $5.1 billion remaining in its reserve and $1.3 billion in cash.

Strategy stock advanced 1.3% to $132.73 on Monday.

The company appears to be executing on a new financial framework unveiled in late June, under which Strategy will opportunistically buy and sell its own shares rather than issuing them continuously. The company has also committed to sell Bitcoin when necessary to pad its dollar reserve.

Bitcoin faces a crucial test on Tuesday as the Senate votes on whether to advance the Clarity Act to floor consideration. If passed, the legislation would place Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies under commodity regulations rather than securities laws. The market has rallied ahead of the decision, with Bitcoin gaining more than 20% over the past month.

data.title: Cooper Stock Dropped and Put Volume Soared Before Bad News. What Happened? — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Andrew Bary

There was unusual trading activity in Cooper Cos. stock before the medical-devices company announced two disappointing developments after the close of trading on Wednesday.

The drop in share price late in the session and heavy put option buying suggest that an investor or investors anticipated two pieces of news: Cooper's decision not to sell a business unit and a cut in its earnings and sales outlook.

It's also possible word got out before the company disclosed the news in two news releases that were released about 4:15 p.m. Eastern Time-and investors traded on it.

Cooper didn't respond to requests for comment.

Cooper, a leading maker of contact lenses, surprised Wall Street by opting not to sell its women's health and fertility business, CooperSurgical, after raising investor expectations about a disposition on its earnings conference call in June. The guidance cut was for its current fiscal year ending in October.

On Wednesday, the stock started to drop just after 2:30 p.m. on heavier-than-usual volume, falling 5% from $67 a share to $63.48 at the market's close at 4 p.m. On Thursday, the stock fell 15% to $54.17 after hitting a new 52-week low in the session.

In coverage of the price drop on Thursday, Barron's wrote that Cooper "sprung a surprise that no one saw coming."

Total volume was 9.5 million shares on Wednesday, up from 2.9 million on Tuesday and an average of under 2 million a day in the previous ior 30 days.

Put option activity stands out. It totaled more than 11,000 contracts on Wednesday, by far the highest volume in five years and up from an average of under 100 contracts a day in the prior three months leading up to last week. The put activity is equivalent to 1.1 million shares with each call and put contract covering 100 shares.

Put options amount to a bearish bet on a stock, giving investors the opportunity to sell the stock at a fixed price.

There often is active trading in a stock and stock options before a major earnings or corporate announcement.

So the trading action in Cooper simply could represent a correct bet by some investors that the news would be bad. There also could have been hedging activity by investors who held the stock in case the news was unfavorable.

One option trade that looks like a hedge was the simultaneous sale of 2,000 September call options with a strike price of $75 a share and the purchase of 2,000 contracts of the September 60-65 strike put spread.

That combined trade is a winner now with Cooper stock under $60 both on the call and put sides of the trade. This trade was highlighted by Susquehanna Financial Group on Wednesday.

Still, the heavy trading and the high put volume indicate the possibility that someone knew about the Cooper news before it became public and traded on it.

The Securities and Exchange Commission didn't respond to a request for comment.

On Monday, shares were trading at $54.64, up 1.4%.

data.title: Brian Moynihan Says Investment Banking Revenues Are Down at BofA — WSJ
data.description:
By Gina Heeb

Bank of America Chief Executive Brian Moynihan said Monday that investment-banking revenue would fall by 10% in the quarter from a year earlier.

"We're not as well positioned in some of the businesses that ... had more activity," Moynihan said at a financial conference hosted by Barclays. He said the bank should bring in about $1.6 billion to $1.8 billion in investment-banking fees, down from about $2 billion a year ago. He said trading revenues would be flat from a year earlier but that still counted as "one of the better third quarters we've ever had."

Moynihan was overall confident in the status of the economy and said future deals are coming. The bank's shares were down more than 5%, falling harder than rivals on Monday.

data.title: The Fed may be on the verge of a serious mistake, prominent economists warn
data.description:
By Greg Robb

Some economists are calling on the central bank to wait before raising interest rates, out of concern the economy may be vulnerable beneath the surface

Traders see a 92% chance that the Federal Reserve, led by Kevin Warsh, will increase interest rates at its meeting this week.

Investors on Wall Street and observers of the Federal Reserve in Washington largely expect the central bank to raise interest rates when it meets this week, but some prominent economists are warning that such a move could prove to be a mistake.

They see the economy as more vulnerable to a steep slowdown in growth than commonly believed. The Fed's job is to keep employment steady and inflation under control. If central bank officials raise rates on Wednesday, the goal will be to cool inflation. But these economists worry that a rate hike could cause a sharp cut in economic activity, which could prompt businesses to let go of workers and ultimately lead to a recession.

"The odds of a serious Fed policy mistake are uncomfortably high and rising," warned Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics, in a post on X.

It's hard to slow economic growth without layoffs, rising unemployment and igniting a "self-reinforcing negative cycle," said Zandi, who has advised leading Democrats over the years.

In late August, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh used his remarks at the Jackson Hole economic symposium to signal that he was concerned about inflation trends. He said he wouldn't hesitate to act if the inflation picture worsened.

Ten days ago, investors put the odds of a rate hike at about 50%. But rising diesel prices, renewed tensions in the Middle East and Friday's hotter-than-expected consumer inflation report have convinced traders and economists that Warsh will follow through on his tough talk and raise rates.

Fed officials will meet behind closed doors Tuesday and Wednesday to decide whether to hike interest rates or hold them steady. The Fed's decision will be announced at 2 p.m. Eastern time on Wednesday, and Warsh will hold a press conference at 2:30 p.m.

Carl Tannenbaum, chief economist at Northern Trust, said the argument for raising rates isn't as clear-cut as the markets and many commentators believe, adding that the central bank has no easy options.

While economic activity has remained buoyant in the face of the war and tariffs, he said, "the economy is not invulnerable."

Lower-income households are tapping into savings to keep up with inflation, he noted.

"Holding rates steady would provide additional time to assess whether there are potential cracks in the foundation of the expansion," Tannenbaum said in an email to clients.

Steve Englander, global head of G10 FX Research, said a hike would be premature given the crosscurrents in the inflation data.

He said the correct Fed policy decision would be to stay on hold until these contradictory signals abate.

For the Fed to raise rates and then have to reverse course and cut rates in a few months would be seen as Warsh having "a very unsteady hand on the tiller."

Some economists think the markets have gone too far in pricing in a hike.

Michael Strain, director of economic policy studies at the American Enterprise Institute, said that the market is reading the Fed wrong and that the "center of gravity" among Fed officials still supports keeping rates unchanged.

Without higher energy prices and tariffs, underlying inflation would be closer to 2.5%, not far above the Fed's 2% target, he said.

Although the likelihood of a rate increase has certainly gone up in recent weeks, Michael Pearce, chief U.S. economist at Oxford Economics, said the September decision could still go either way.

"We're sticking with our forecast that the Fed leaves rate on hold," Pearce said in a note to clients.

-Greg Robb

data.title: Stewards Share Fall After Co. Provides Details on Proposed Acquisitions
data.description:
By Stephen Nakrosis

Shares of Stewards are trading lower on the Nasdaq Monday, after the company provided new information on a pair of proposed acquisitions in South Florida.

Shares are down 9% to $2.69. Volume at the time topped 966,000 shares, above the 65-day average volume of 464,266 shares.

In its latest Form 10-Q, the diversified financial platform said it signed non-binding letters of intent to purchase PIXL at Plantation and Envy Pompano Beach, two multifamily properties in Florida.

In connection with the agreement, Stewards received five promissory notes with a value of $1.7 million. The company added certain note balances may be applied against an applicable purchase price if a transaction were to close.

Stewards said under the terms of the proposed deal, it would issue restricted shares of common stock at a price of $3 per share to acquire the existing owners' equity interests in the two properties.

The company added "the $240 million figure represents the aggregate implied value of PIXL and Envy, inclusive of property-level debt, and does not represent the amount of stock consideration to be issued in the proposed acquisitions."

The company's shares began trading on the Nasdaq Capital Market as the result of an uplisting from the OTCID Market on Sept. 10., and closed that day's trading at $2.23.

data.title: Ebola Cases Cross 7,000 In Congo As Outbreak Spreads To 7 Provinces
data.description:
WASHINGTON (dpa-AFX) - The number of confirmed Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has risen to more than 7,000 across seven provinces affected by the outbreak, according to an epidemiological report published Sunday.

Of the total cases officially recorded, 3,398 people have died. At present, 837 people are either being treated or kept in isolation.

The outbreak involves the rare Bundibugyo virus and is the DRC's 17th Ebola outbreak. It began in the northeastern province of Ituri before spreading to remote areas in the east and north of the country.

Earlier this week, Ebola was confirmed in South-Ubangi province, the seventh province affected by the outbreak. The province is in northwestern DRC and borders the Central African Republic and the Republic of Congo. The infected person, a 23-year-old man who had travelled from South Kivu on July 10, later died from the disease.

A government report said that the quality of medical care remains below required standards in some areas because of limited resources and treatment capacity. In parts of Ituri, Ebola treatment centers are overcrowded. In Haut-Uele, one treatment center does not have proper sanitation facilities, while another does not have reliable access to water and electricity.

Healthcare services have also been affected in other provinces. In Tshopo, a shortage of safe blood supplies and technical problems have made patient care more difficult. In Bas-Uele, there are not enough treatment centers or ambulances to provide adequate care.

data.title: Trump Says AI Doesn't Need More Guardrails Despite Industry Warnings — WSJ
data.description:
By Brian Schwartz

President Trump pushed back on the need for tighter federal regulations linked to artificial intelligence, even as industry leaders sound urgent warnings about potential dangers from their own technology.

"The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday. "There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China."

The post is the latest instance of Trump publicly playing down the need for extensive oversight onto AI. His position on additional federal oversight of the AI comes as executives, including his ally Elon Musk, call to slow down advancements of the booming technology out of concern of the risks it could create, in what has become a rapidly escalating crisis for the industry.

Trump's position on AI and data centers contrasts with how many voters feel about the issue heading into the midterms. A March Gallup poll showed that nearly half of those surveyed "strongly oppose" the construction of local AI data centers. And the opposition isn't just coming from Democrats-just under 40% of Republicans polled by Gallup are strongly against the creation of data centers. The outcry has become a mounting political liability for Republicans and some Democrats ahead of the election in November.

"We can put up guardrails, and we can do this and that, but I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up," Trump told reporters Sunday while traveling in Ireland. "And they're bringing up things that won't happen." Trump has also said he uses AI but declined to provide further details.

Anthropic Chief Executive Dario Amodei has been among the lead voices calling to slow down AI's development. Trump said in his post that the administration has taken issue with and moved to stop select AI companies and their leaders from certain actions in the past - singling out Amodei as an example - and would continue to do so.

In a post to his personal blog, Amodei called for the AI industry to pace development of cutting-edge tools, suggesting new measures including more global coordination among democratic countries and the introduction of embedded third-party safety evaluators.

"I believe that if slowing down bought us even an extra year or two before models reach critical levels of capability, and we used that time to advance alignment, we could greatly reduce the risk that something goes seriously wrong," he wrote.

Anthropic and the Trump administration have been clashing for months. Anthropic sued the administration after the Pentagon marked the company as a supply chain risk, and argued the Pentagon illegally retaliated against the company for its standing on artificial intelligence safety. A federal judge recently ruled in favor of Anthropic and found the administration's actions were unlawful.

An Anthropic researcher, Jacob Coxon, recently said he was quitting the artificial-intelligence industry over fears that the lab and its competitors are racing to build systems they won't be able to control, a sign of mounting safety concerns within top AI companies.

Coxon, who specializes in training new AI models by having them consume vast amounts of data, said he doesn't want to participate in an industrywide rush to build AI systems that can improve themselves, worried such systems could spiral out of control and destroy humanity.

Other tech companies have signaled a need for caution. Microsoft published a provisional code of conduct that it aims to apply when training new AI models. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also warned that the dizzying pace of progress could go "very badly" and that humans could lose "control of the future to AI."

"We welcome a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements for frontier AI," Altman said in a post on X. "No amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness."

Separately on Monday, Vice President JD Vance told reporters the administration needs to "regulate smartly" but that he wasn't in favor of companies requesting additional safeguards.

"I feel a little bit weird about the fact that you have so many frontier AI tech companies kind of coming to the government and begging the government to regulate them," Vance said.

Write to Brian Schwartz at brian.schwartz@wsj.com

data.title: Swiss Market Ends On Firm Note
data.description:
BRUSSELS (dpa-AFX) - The Switzerland market ended on a strong note on Monday after holding firm right through the day's session thanks to sustained buying at several counters.

Despite lingering concerns about geopolitical tensions and elevated oil prices, the mood in the Swiss market remained quite positive.

The benchmark SMI settled with a gain of 103.27 points or 0.75% at 13,878.54, after moving between 13,829.94 and 13,998.88.

Roche moved up 5%. Lindt & Spruengli, Nestle, Alcon, Kuehne + Nagel and Novartis climbed 1.7%-2.2%.

Sonova, Givaudan, Straumann Holding, Swisscom, Zurich Insurance and Swiss Re gained 1%-1.5%. Lonza Group, Galderma Group and Schindler Ps posted modest gains.

VAT Group dropped 7.65%. ABB dropped about 4.1%. UBS Group, Holcim, Sika, Amrize, Logitech International, Richemont and Partners Group also ended notably lower.

In economic news, Switzerland's producer and import prices increased for the first time in four months in August, the Federal Statistical Office reported.

The producer and import price index posted a monthly increase of 0.7% in August, reversing a 0.1% decrease in July. That was faster than the 0.1% rise expected by economists.

The producer price index decreased 1.3% from last month, while import prices climbed 0.8%.

On a yearly basis, the decline in producer and import prices eased to 0.7% from 2.1% in July.

data.title: Micron Stock Sinks Again. What AI Safety Fears Mean for Memory Chips. — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Adam Clark

It looks like another day of pain for Micron Technology, with the memory-chip stock on the sharp end of worries about reduced artificial-intelligence infrastructure investment. But there's no real evidence yet of an AI pause.

Micron shares were down 5.8% at $919.18 in early trading Monday. Added to losses from last week, the stock is set to lose all of its September gains in September.

American depositary receipts of peer SK Hynix were falling 5.8%.

Micron is a volatile stock, having risen more than sixfold in the past 12 months, and it reacts sharply to anything that indicates a slowdown in AI spending.

The latest worry is the bosses of Anthropic, OpenAI, and SpaceX all calling for a slowdown in AI development over the weekend.

That would be pretty bad for the memory-chip market, as AI hardware has driven a supply shortage and soaring prices. Analysts at UBS estimate that out of a nearly $1 trillion increase in AI capital expenditure between 2025 and 2027, around 90% is set to be spent on memory. A true pause in the technology would put all of that at risk.

"We now expect AI capex to reach nearly $1 trillion this year and around $1.4 trillion by 2027," wrote UBS economist Arend Kapyteyn in a research note. "An increasing share of that spending is being absorbed by memory costs, reflecting in part the sharp rise in memory prices this year and the further increases expected next year."

Lucky for Micron, then, that we still seem to be a way off from anyone actually stopping construction of data centers. The most concrete measure so far has been Claude developer Anthropic's commitment to allowing third-party evaluators access to its systems. Meanwhile, the company appears to be steaming ahead with plans for an initial public offering that could value the company at $2 trillion-not exactly a sign that spending is about to stop.

Nancy Tengler, CEO and CIO at Laffer Tengler Investments, said she was using the weakness to add to her position in Micron.

"The AI build-out backlog is in place, and these data centers are being built. That that will continue to drive growth for some time," Tengler said. "What the stock market is concerned about, obviously, is where are we two to three years out. I think we will still be in a buildout that's a once in a generation technological revolution."

So far, the Trump administration is still backing the data-center buildout, and no AI executive has said they would reduce their capex spending. A more immediate issue might be high borrowing costs as markets bet on the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates this week.

But Micron has weathered AI spending concerns before, and so far this looks just like another bout of volatility.
